item.title: Local LLMs for Text Translation — A Benchmark on RTX 5060 Ti with 16GB VRAM
item.description:
I recently wanted to test the quality of AI models for translation. I've already translated quite a few books and texts using cloud models like Qwen, Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini, and I'm increasingly satisfied with the results. I don't think translators need to look for new jobs just yet, but the reality today is that you can translate any book in any language into Russian and at least understand what it's about. Of course, nuances of style, language subtleties, and local life realities remain crucial for translating complex fiction, requiring that 'life context' that models lack. However, the latest versions of Claude and OpenAI have become quite adept at translating authorial style. If you need to read texts that aren't necessarily highly specialized, AI translation will likely satisfy you. There are still subtleties, of course—checks and prompts—but that's a matter of technique, solvable with skills and token budget. Yet, cloud translations aren't always accessible due to budget and copyright policies (and it's unclear how long they'll remain available), so I wondered how much I could rely on local models running on a modest setup by today's standards: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, Core Ultra 7 265, 96 GB DDR5. Translations were checked for various languages, all translated into Russian. To make the benchmark more representative, I chose several languages for testing: English, Spanish, Chinese, and Hebrew. I know most of them, so I can evaluate the translation visually, although it wasn't necessary. The reference translation was done with Claude models, then 'judge models' (Claude and OpenAI) evaluated each translation, assigning a score. Both translation quality and speed were measured. item.title: How I Built an AI Workbench for an Analyst in an IT Company
item.description:
At that point, I was already using agents in my own work: connecting different models, organizing mutual checks, accumulating experience between sessions. I had experience implementing corporate systems, so training and support were not new to me. Now I had to assemble an analyst's workbench that would provide a different speed of creating software documentation. Along with the tools, I had to transfer the way of working: how to set a task, check the result, get help, and save the found solution for others. As implementation progressed, roles and skills were added: canon owner, update releases, messenger support, and several memory levels. In the article, I will explain what problems required these solutions and what had to be reconsidered along the way. Read more

item.title: How I Crossed RAG, LLM, and RandomForest: An Architecture for Trading Signals with Evidence
item.description:
In the first part, I discussed how I built a RAG system with a LangGraph agent on local LLMs. It could search for news, answer questions, and extract entities. But for trading, this is not enough – you need to not just read, but predict. In this article, I will explain how I turned a news scraper into an ML pipeline that generates trading signals (BUY/SELL/NEUTRAL) with evidence. We will go from linking news to tickers to an Explainable UI, analyze pitfalls with small data, and look into the project's architectural future. Stack: Scikit-learn, Plotly, FastAPI, Streamlit, PostgreSQL, Ollama. Read more

item.title: How an AI assistant gets 1C context and checks extensions
item.description:
A large language model doesn't know how a specific information base is structured. It cannot see configuration modules, active extensions, user rights, or document data until it gains controlled access. Therefore, the practical task isn't just choosing a model. It's about gathering relevant context for it, limiting its actions, and incorporating result verification. item.title: Most AI Agents Are the Same Inside. So What's the Difference?
item.description:
Imagine: a technical specification on the table and three contractor proposals. Prices are for different periods, some conditions are in appendices, one proposal is missing an obligatory work item. You need to read everything, compare, recalculate under the same conditions, and prepare a memo with sources. You can ask an AI to explain how to do this, or you can give it documents and tools and assign the work itself: let it read, compare, calculate, and return the result. In the second case, the model is already managing the task execution. This is an agent. Under the hood, it's a familiar loop: the model selects a tool and call parameters, ordinary code executes the tool, and the result is returned to the model. And so on. This principle—reason, act, observe the result—is the basis of ReAct. An engine and four wheels are present in both a truck and a car, but they are not interchangeable. The same applies to agents: all the interesting stuff starts with questions that didn't make it into the pseudocode. -Is the proposed command even executable? —What to do if the tool returns a gigabyte of text? —How to continue working when the context window is full? —Is the model's phrase "done" enough to close the task? All this is assembled into a harness—the agent's execution environment: the loop, tools, memory, checks, limits, and action history. This is where most of the engineering work lies. We at GigaCode R&D develop models for agent tasks. We needed an executor with which we could experiment, get training data, and solve applied problems. Thus, GigaCode Universal Agent was born—an open-source Python project with model connections via chat/completions API. We'll explain what surrounds the agent loop and how a single core is used for working with documents, code, and external systems. Read more

item.title: How to Separate Author Assistance from Scientific Work Substitution
item.description:
An article discusses a case where a Science publication contained a significant error (2.1 billion white herons, exceeding the global population) due to a data entry mistake (2^31 - 1). The author explores whether AI could have detected such errors before publication and concludes that while AI can assist in checking data consistency, references, and code, it cannot replace human judgment in assessing data suitability or defining 'normal' in a subject area. The article introduces two tools, Domate (for plagiarism and AI detection) and Dotrace (an AI-assisted editor for academic writing), and proposes developing AI presets for specific checks like bibliography verification, arithmetic control, logical consistency, and skeptical review to enhance research quality and train researchers in critical self-assessment, while emphasizing that ultimate responsibility remains with the human author.
